phy-resp-051.why: Inspiration requires expansion of the thorax. The diaphragm contracts and descends while the external intercostals elevate the ribs. Alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric pressure and air enters.

notes.A: The diaphragm moves upward when it relaxes during quiet expiration.
notes.B: External intercostal contraction lifts the ribs and increases the transverse and anteroposterior dimensions of the chest.
notes.C: A contracting diaphragm descends and increases the vertical dimension of the thorax.
notes.D: The rib movement is correct, but the diaphragm moves down during active inspiration.

phy-resp-052.why: The transpulmonary pressure is alveolar pressure minus intrapleural pressure. A positive transpulmonary pressure distends the lung and counteracts its inward recoil.

notes.B: Pleural pressure is normally subatmospheric at rest. A positive pressure without a comparable alveolar pressure can compress the lung.
notes.C: In quiet breathing, pleural pressure is below atmospheric pressure during both inspiration and expiration.
notes.D: Pleural pressure swings vary with respiratory effort, but the distending pressure depends on the difference between alveolar and pleural pressures.
notes.E: Equal pleural and atmospheric pressures can occur in an open pneumothorax, where the lung can lose its distending pressure.

phy-resp-055.why: Within the normal tracheobronchial tree, the medium-sized bronchi contribute the greatest resistance. Small airways have narrow individual lumens, but there are very many in parallel, which lowers their combined resistance.

notes.A: The oral opening can contribute resistance, but the standard intrathoracic airway comparison concerns the branches downstream of the trachea.
notes.B: The main bronchi are wide, so their large radii decrease resistance in ordinary breathing.
notes.D: Individual small airways can have high resistance, but their arrangement in parallel lowers their total resistance.
notes.E: Alveoli provide a large surface for diffusion and are not the major site of resistance to bulk airflow.

phy-resp-059.why: Vital capacity is the volume that can be expelled after a maximal inspiration. It includes the inspiratory reserve, one tidal breath and the expiratory reserve, leaving residual volume behind.

notes.A: Tidal volume is the amount moved in one quiet breath and is included in vital capacity.
notes.B: Expiratory reserve volume is the additional air that can be exhaled after a normal expiration and is included.
notes.C: Residual volume stays in the lungs after maximal expiration, so it cannot be part of the volume expelled.
notes.D: Inspiratory reserve volume is the additional air that can be inhaled after a normal inspiration and is included.

phy-resp-060.why: Quiet inspiration is active. Contraction of the diaphragm expands the thorax vertically, and external intercostal activity helps lift the ribs. Quiet expiration is usually driven by elastic recoil.

notes.A: The abdominal muscles are recruited chiefly during forced expiration, coughing or other efforts.
notes.B: External intercostals help elevate and stabilise the ribs during inspiration.
notes.C: The diaphragm is the main inspiratory muscle and contracts during quiet breathing.
notes.D: Pectoral muscles can help during laboured inspiration when the shoulder girdle is fixed, but they are not primary quiet-breathing muscles.

phy-resp-066.why: Pulmonary surfactant lowers the surface tension at the alveolar air–liquid interface. This lowers the pressure needed to expand the lung and increases compliance.

notes.A: Surfactant is produced by type II pneumocytes. Type I cells provide most of the thin gas exchange surface.
notes.B: The surface-active film decreases surface tension, especially as alveoli become smaller.
notes.C: Pleural pressure depends on chest wall and lung mechanics. Surfactant does not make it positive during quiet breathing.
notes.D: The principal effect is on alveolar surface mechanics. Pulmonary blood flow is not normally reduced as its direct function.

phy-resp-068.why: The diaphragm is the principal muscle of inspiration. External intercostals contribute by elevating and stabilising the ribs, while most forced expiratory muscles are recruited only as demand rises.

notes.A: Most interosseous internal intercostals contribute to forced expiration, although parasternal portions may assist inspiration.
notes.C: Abdominal muscles can raise intra-abdominal pressure and help drive forced expiration.
notes.D: Serratus posterior inferior is not one of the principal muscles needed for ordinary inspiration.
notes.E: The list includes muscles used mainly during active expiration or with additional demand.

phy-resp-070.why: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant, a lipid-rich film containing phospholipids and specific proteins, some of which carry carbohydrate groups. By decreasing surface tension, the film stabilises alveoli at low volume and limits forces that favour alveolar flooding.

notes.A: Type II pneumocytes synthesise and secrete surfactant from lamellar bodies.
notes.B: Phospholipids provide the main surface-active component. Surfactant also contains neutral lipids and proteins, including glycosylated proteins.
notes.C: As an alveolus gets smaller, the surfactant film becomes more concentrated at its surface and lowers tension further.
notes.D: Lower surface tension helps prevent alveolar collapse and decreases the forces that favour fluid entering air spaces.

phy-resp-073.why: Eupnoea is quiet, comfortable breathing at rest, with a regular rhythm and no unusual respiratory effort. Rate and depth can increase during normal exercise without necessarily producing dyspnoea.

notes.A: Polypnoea typically refers to increased frequency of breathing and sometimes increased ventilation.
notes.C: Tachypnoea is an abnormally rapid breathing rate for the person and circumstances.
notes.D: Dyspnoea is the subjective experience of uncomfortable or difficult breathing.
notes.E: Hyperpnoea is deeper or greater ventilation, as occurs when metabolic demand rises during exercise.

phy-resp-074.why: During quiet expiration, the diaphragm relaxes and rises as the respiratory system recoils. Pleural pressure becomes less negative, while alveolar pressure briefly exceeds atmospheric pressure and drives air out.

notes.A: Relaxation of the diaphragm allows its dome to rise while elastic recoil decreases thoracic volume.
notes.B: Pleural pressure becomes more negative during inspiration, then reverses direction during expiration.
notes.C: Pleural pressure rises toward its less negative value at end expiration.
notes.D: The rib cage recoils, but pleural pressure rises rather than falls during quiet expiration.

phy-resp-076.why: Tidal volume is the air moved in one breath. A representative value for a resting adult is about 500 millilitres, with variation according to body size and ventilatory demand.

notes.A: Air moved per minute is minute ventilation, calculated as tidal volume multiplied by breathing frequency.
notes.B: Residual volume is the air left after maximal expiration and usually exceeds a quiet tidal volume.
notes.C: Functional residual capacity is expiratory reserve volume plus residual volume.
notes.D: Minute ventilation, residual volume and functional residual capacity describe different quantities from one tidal breath.

phy-resp-077.why: In quiet breathing, pleural pressure is normally below atmospheric pressure because lung recoil pulls inward and the chest wall tends to spring outward. Lung recoil reflects both tissue elasticity and alveolar surface tension.

notes.A: Pleural pressure can become positive during forced expiration, but that does not describe normal quiet breathing.
notes.B: Normal resting lung and chest wall recoil create a subatmospheric pressure in the sealed pleural space.
notes.C: Pleural pressure can approach atmospheric pressure after communication with the outside air, as in an open pneumothorax.
notes.D: Elastic tissue and alveolar surface tension both contribute to inward pulmonary recoil, which helps determine pleural pressure.

phy-resp-078.why: Anatomical dead space is the volume of the conducting airways, where inspired air is transported without exchanging gas with blood. In a typical adult it is around 140–150 millilitres and varies with body size.

notes.A: Alveoli are beyond the anatomical dead space. Poorly perfused alveoli can add to physiological dead space.
notes.B: Most gas exchange occurs across perfused alveoli rather than in the conducting airways.
notes.D: About 500 millilitres is a representative tidal volume, which includes both conducting-airway and alveolar portions.
notes.E: Litres per minute measure flow or ventilation rate. Anatomical dead space is a volume.

phy-resp-079.why: Residual volume is the gas still in the lungs after the strongest possible expiration. It cannot be breathed out into a spirometer and is calculated from a measurement that includes trapped lung gas.

notes.B: The volume in the lungs after maximal inspiration is total lung capacity, which includes residual volume.
notes.C: A typical young adult residual volume is closer to about 1–1.5 litres, though values vary with age, size and lung disease.
notes.D: Tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume gives inspiratory capacity, the amount that can be inhaled after a normal expiration.
notes.E: Vital capacity includes only volumes that can be moved during a maximal breath.

phy-resp-575.why: Vital capacity equals tidal volume plus inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes. Residual volume cannot be exhaled and is not included, so adding it in place of inspiratory reserve is incorrect.

notes.A: The tidal breath and the two reserve volumes together form the maximum movable air volume.
notes.B: Predicted vital capacity depends on age, sex and height, among other factors.
notes.C: Thoracic dimensions and body size influence predicted lung volumes, including vital capacity.
notes.D: Inspiratory capacity is tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve, so adding expiratory reserve gives vital capacity.

phy-resp-576.why: Smooth muscle is present in the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles. Changing its tone adjusts airway calibre and can markedly change resistance to flow.

notes.A: The external lung surface is covered by visceral pleura. Airway smooth muscle is mainly arranged within the walls of conducting airways.
notes.B: The medial surface includes the hilum, where structures enter and leave. Airway smooth muscle is in the walls of the airways themselves.
notes.D: The thin alveolar septa provide a gas exchange surface. There is no continuous smooth muscle coat around individual alveoli.
notes.E: The two lung surfaces are covered by visceral pleura. Neither describes the characteristic distribution of bronchial smooth muscle.

phy-resp-578.why: Elastic fibres form a supporting network throughout the lung. They support alveolar septa and small airways and are present in the connective tissue of visceral pleura, allowing recoil after inflation.

notes.A: Alveolar septa contain elastic fibres that stretch with inflation and contribute to recoil during expiration.
notes.B: Connective tissue around small distal airways contains fibres that help tether the airways to surrounding lung.
notes.C: Visceral pleura covers the external and medial lung surfaces and contains elastic connective tissue.
notes.D: Elastic tissue is also present in the visceral pleura, beyond the alveolar and airway structures listed here.

phy-resp-583.why: In typical inspiration the diaphragm contracts, flattens and descends, increasing the vertical thoracic dimension. It rises when it relaxes during expiration.

notes.A: External intercostals help elevate the ribs, enlarging the thoracic cavity.
notes.C: Elevation of the anterior ribs and sternum increases the front-to-back dimension.
notes.D: Upward and outward movement of the lateral ribs increases chest width.
notes.E: The scalene and sternocleidomastoid muscles can assist inspiration when ventilatory effort rises.

phy-resp-584.why: Total lung capacity is the gas volume in the lungs after a maximal inspiration. Around six litres is a conventional value for an adult man, with substantial variation by height, age and individual factors.

notes.A: Around 4.2 litres may be appropriate for a smaller person or for another capacity. It is below the typical teaching value in adult men.
notes.B: Around 1.5 litres is closer to a usual residual volume or a reserve volume than total lung capacity.
notes.D: Eight litres is above the typical estimate but can occur in a particularly large person or with hyperinflation.
notes.E: Ten litres is much higher than the conventional adult value and would not be the usual estimate.

phy-resp-589.why: Pulmonary surfactant sits at the alveolar air–liquid interface and reduces surface tension. This decreases the pressure needed for inflation and helps alveoli remain open as their volume falls.

notes.A: Surfactant helps prevent collapse and reduces the pressure work of reopening alveoli rather than obstructing expiration.
notes.C: Relaxation of bronchi mainly depends on airway smooth muscle signalling. Surfactant acts chiefly at the alveolar interface.
notes.D: Secretion can respond to lung stretch and several signalling pathways. Increased sympathetic tone is not the defining action being tested.
notes.E: By lowering surface tension, surfactant tends to oppose forces that favour fluid movement into alveoli.

phy-resp-594.why: Surfactant reduces the surface tension that opposes lung expansion. Thus a given change in transpulmonary pressure can produce a greater volume change, which means pulmonary compliance increases.

notes.A: Surfactant lowers the surface tension at the alveolar lining, rather than increasing it.
notes.C: As alveolar surface area falls during expiration, the surfactant film becomes more closely packed and can reduce tension more effectively.
notes.D: Interruption of pulmonary perfusion is not a usual stimulus that raises the amount of surfactant.
notes.E: Surfactant chiefly alters alveolar surface forces. It does not increase resistance in the conducting bronchi.

phy-resp-596.why: Alveolar pressure is slightly subatmospheric during quiet inspiration, with its lowest value near peak inspiratory flow. At end inspiration, airflow stops as alveolar pressure returns toward atmospheric pressure.

notes.A: Pleural pressure usually becomes progressively more negative as lung volume rises, reaching its minimum near end inspiration.
notes.C: Oesophageal pressure is used as a surrogate for pleural pressure. Its inspiratory minimum is generally nearer end inspiration.
notes.D: Airflow is near zero at end inspiration because the pressure gradient between atmosphere and alveoli has largely disappeared.
notes.E: Hysteresis is the difference between the pressure–volume paths followed during inflation and deflation.

phy-resp-602.why: In spontaneous inspiration, the fall in intrathoracic pressure increases the pressure gradient for systemic venous return to the right heart. Left ventricular filling can briefly behave differently as pulmonary vessels accommodate blood.

notes.B: Quiet expiration mostly uses elastic recoil, while active muscle contraction supplies energy for inspiration.
notes.C: Surface tension tends to shrink alveoli and opposes inflation. Surfactant reduces this opposing force.
notes.D: Pleural pressure is already below atmospheric pressure before quiet inspiration. A further fall increases transpulmonary distending pressure.
notes.E: Alveolar expansion spreads the surfactant film over a larger area, decreasing its surface concentration.

phy-resp-603.why: Residual volume is the air remaining after maximal expiration. It is not exhaled during a spirometric manoeuvre and requires an indirect method, such as a lung-volume measurement by plethysmography.

notes.B: Predicted absolute residual volume depends on age, sex and height. It is generally higher in men of similar age.
notes.C: A usual young-adult value is closer to 1–1.5 litres. Higher residual volume can occur with marked air trapping.
notes.D: Spirometry records air moved into or out of the mouth. It cannot directly record the gas left after maximal expiration.
notes.E: Residual volume often increases with age as elastic recoil decreases and airways close at higher lung volumes.

phy-resp-609.why: Compliance is the change in volume divided by the change in distending pressure. It is the slope of the pressure–volume relation and varies with the volume range and the properties of the lung and chest wall.

notes.B: Compliance is generally greater in the mid-volume operating range and falls near high lung volumes.
notes.C: Alveolar surface tension increases inward recoil and makes the lung harder to distend, reducing compliance.
notes.D: Surfactant decreases surface tension and usually increases lung compliance.
notes.E: A parallel shift changes the position of the curve but preserves its slope, which is the measure of compliance.

phy-resp-615.why: When air enters the pleural space, pleural pressure can approach atmospheric pressure. The reduced transpulmonary distending pressure allows the lung to recoil inward, while the chest wall tends to spring outward.

notes.B: In a simple pneumothorax the lung recoils because it loses distending pressure. Direct compression is more relevant to tension pneumothorax.
notes.C: The affected lung loses aerated volume as it recoils. A rise in functional residual capacity is not the typical result.
notes.D: Loss of the inward pull exerted by the lung allows the chest wall to recoil outward.
notes.E: Collapse decreases the volume that can be ventilated and can reduce vital capacity.

phy-resp-616.why: Emphysema destroys elastic tissue and weakens small-airway tethering. Airways can close earlier during expiration, trapping gas and raising residual volume. This can reduce the volume that can be exhaled after a maximal inspiration.

notes.A: Destruction of some alveolar capillary beds can increase physiological dead space through poorly perfused ventilation.
notes.B: The defining structural change is loss of alveolar walls and elastic tissue. Reduced surfactant is not the main mechanical defect.
notes.C: Expiratory airway collapse tends to increase residual volume through air trapping.
notes.E: Pleural pressure varies with respiratory phase and force. The consistent mechanical change is loss of lung elastic recoil.

phy-resp-617.why: Once a bronchus is completely obstructed, fresh gas cannot reach its alveoli. Gas already there is gradually absorbed into blood, reducing alveolar volume and causing resorption atelectasis.

notes.B: Bronchial obstruction does not directly admit air into the pleural cavity or raise pleural pressure as a primary event.
notes.C: The obstructed region is perfused but poorly ventilated, which causes shunt or low ventilation–perfusion matching rather than dead space.
notes.D: Low alveolar oxygen triggers pulmonary arteriolar constriction and tends to divert blood away from the affected region.
notes.E: Cyanosis can occur with severe hypoxaemia, but regional collapse is the more direct and usual consequence.

phy-resp-626.why: Air flows from higher to lower pressure. During inspiration, thoracic expansion lowers alveolar pressure slightly below atmospheric pressure, drawing air into the lungs.

notes.A: Alveolar pressure above atmospheric pressure drives air out, as during expiration.
notes.C: Equal alveolar and atmospheric pressures provide no pressure gradient for net airflow.
notes.D: The diaphragm normally contracts and descends, increasing thoracic volume and lowering alveolar pressure.
notes.E: External intercostal contraction can assist inspiration by elevating the ribs. Relaxation is not required to draw air in.

phy-resp-629.why: If the manoeuvre starts at the end of a normal expiration, the extra air that can be exhaled by maximal effort is expiratory reserve volume. Residual volume is what remains afterwards.

notes.A: Tidal volume is the air moved during the normal breath itself, without the additional forced expiration.
notes.C: Peak expiratory flow is a rate, measured as volume per unit time. The amount expelled here is a volume.
notes.D: Eupnoea is quiet breathing at rest and does not include the additional forced manoeuvre.
notes.E: Inspiratory reserve volume is the extra air that can be inhaled after a normal inspiration.

phy-resp-631.why: Cohesive forces at the alveolar air–liquid interface create surface tension that tends to shrink the surface. This adds to inward elastic recoil. Surfactant lowers this tension and stabilises alveoli at small volumes.

notes.A: Surface tension increases the tendency of an alveolus to shrink or collapse, particularly when surfactant is deficient.
notes.B: Untreated surface tension increases the pressure needed to expand the lung and therefore decreases compliance.
notes.D: Surface tension acts inward as the lung recoils. It is the inflation of the lung that must overcome this force.
notes.E: Surface tension is a mechanical property, not a direct barrier to diffusion. Severe collapse due to high tension can secondarily reduce gas exchange.

phy-resp-635.why: An adult often exhales about four fifths of forced vital capacity in the first second. FEV1/FVC varies with age and should be compared with an appropriate lower limit of normal for clinical interpretation.

notes.A: A ratio of 95 percent can occur, but it is above the usual teaching estimate for a healthy adult.
notes.C: A ratio of 65 percent may be low, particularly in younger adults, and is not the typical adult estimate.
notes.D: Expelling only half the forced vital capacity in one second is well below the usual healthy adult ratio.
notes.E: A ratio of 40 percent indicates a much smaller early expired fraction and is not a typical healthy value.

phy-resp-637.why: During normal quiet inspiration, pleural pressure is below atmospheric pressure and becomes more negative as the thorax expands. The resulting rise in transpulmonary pressure helps inflate the lungs.

notes.A: Positive pleural pressure can occur with forceful expiration or applied positive pressure. It is not usual during spontaneous quiet inspiration.
notes.C: Pleural pressure remains subatmospheric throughout quiet breathing, including the usual pauses when alveolar pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
notes.D: Alveolar surface tension contributes to lung recoil, which helps determine pleural pressure together with chest wall mechanics.
notes.E: A break in the pleural seal can admit air and allow pleural pressure to approach atmospheric pressure.

phy-resp-639.why: Type II pneumocytes synthesise and store surfactant in lamellar bodies before secreting it into the alveolar lining. The surfactant film lowers surface tension and helps stabilise alveoli.

notes.B: Type I pneumocytes form the thin surface specialised for gas diffusion. They are not the main source of alveolar surfactant.
notes.C: Airway goblet cells secrete mucins into the conducting airways. They do not produce the main alveolar surfactant film.
notes.D: Pulmonary vessels carry blood to the gas exchange surface. The surfactant is produced by alveolar epithelial cells.
notes.E: Bronchial smooth muscle changes airway calibre. It does not secrete the alveolar surfactant film.

phy-resp-641.why: Asthma increases airway resistance through bronchial smooth muscle contraction, mucosal swelling and mucus. These changes narrow the airway lumen and particularly limit expiratory flow.

notes.B: Emphysema reduces airway tethering and can increase expiratory resistance or flow limitation as small airways narrow.
notes.C: Paraplegia can weaken the muscles of forced expiration and coughing. This does not by itself imply increased airway resistance.
notes.D: More resistance requires a larger pressure difference to produce the same airflow, increasing the work of breathing.
notes.E: Airway resistance rises when asthma narrows airway calibre and falls when the obstruction improves.

phy-resp-643.why: At the end of a quiet expiration, inward lung recoil is balanced by outward chest wall recoil. The sealed pleural space is typically about 5 centimetres of water below atmosphere, equivalent to roughly −4 mm Hg.

notes.B: Positive four millimetres of mercury is inconsistent with the usual subatmospheric pleural pressure at rest.
notes.C: A value around minus six millimetres of mercury is closer to the more negative pressure reached during ordinary inspiration.
notes.D: Positive six millimetres of mercury can only reflect different mechanics, such as an active expiratory effort, rather than quiet resting conditions.
notes.E: A pleural pressure near minus ten millimetres of mercury may occur with deeper inspiration but is below the usual quiet end-expiratory level.

phy-resp-650.why: Pulmonary ventilation is bulk movement of air between the atmosphere and lungs. Inspiration brings air in and expiration moves it out. The gases subsequently diffuse across the alveolar–capillary interface.

notes.A: Expiration moves air out, but it is only one part of the complete ventilatory cycle.
notes.B: Inspiration moves air into the lungs and is followed by the outward flow of expiration.
notes.D: Transfer across the alveolar–capillary membrane is gas exchange by diffusion rather than ventilation.
notes.E: Circulation transports gases in blood between the lungs and tissues. This is distinct from moving air through the airways.

phy-resp-651.why: As inspiratory muscles expand the thorax, intrapleural pressure becomes more negative. This increases transpulmonary pressure, expanding the lungs and briefly reducing alveolar pressure below atmospheric pressure.

notes.A: Stretching the alveolar film generally spreads the surfactant and can increase surface tension as the alveolus expands.
notes.B: The chest volume rises as the diaphragm contracts and moves downward.
notes.C: Tidal volume is the amount of air exchanged per breath. Its change depends on ventilatory effort, not on inspiration itself.
notes.D: Alveolar pressure decreases at the onset of quiet inspiration and returns toward atmospheric pressure at the end.

phy-resp-069.why: Epinephrine activates beta-2 receptors and relaxes airway smooth muscle. Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and can relieve bronchoconstriction sustained by vagal acetylcholine. Both mechanisms increase airway calibre.

notes.A: Epinephrine activates beta-2 signalling, which promotes airway relaxation. The paired option also includes muscarinic blockade.
notes.B: Atropine prevents acetylcholine from maintaining muscarinic bronchoconstrictor tone. The paired option also includes a beta-2 agonist.
notes.D: Histamine and bradykinin can cause bronchoconstriction in susceptible airways rather than producing the relaxation sought here.
notes.E: Acetylcholine increases airway smooth muscle tone through muscarinic M3 receptors.

phy-resp-072.why: Circulating epinephrine can activate beta-2 receptors on airway smooth muscle. The resulting rise in cyclic AMP favours relaxation and increases bronchial calibre.

notes.B: Lower catecholamine activity reduces the opportunity for beta-2-mediated bronchial relaxation rather than increasing it.
notes.C: Acetylcholine promotes muscarinic contraction, and serotonin can constrict airways under some conditions.
notes.D: Histamine and bradykinin can support bronchoconstrictor responses, especially in hyperresponsive airways.
notes.E: This list includes mediators that can contract bronchial smooth muscle alongside the beta-2-mediated dilator stimulus.

phy-resp-075.why: Bronchodilation from adrenergic stimulation is mediated mainly by beta-2 receptors on airway smooth muscle. In humans, circulating epinephrine is important because direct sympathetic innervation of that muscle is limited.

notes.A: Alpha receptors have important vascular actions. Airway smooth muscle relaxation is predominantly a beta-2 response.
notes.C: Muscarinic receptors mediate the parasympathetic airway response, including contraction through the M3 subtype.
notes.D: Nicotinic receptors mediate ganglionic transmission but are not the main adrenergic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle.
notes.E: H2 is a histamine receptor, not an adrenergic receptor. It does not mediate the standard sympathetic bronchodilator response.

phy-resp-592.why: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors. Blocking acetylcholine signalling at M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle reduces vagal bronchoconstrictor tone, so airway calibre can increase.

notes.A: Nicotinic receptors are important for autonomic ganglionic transmission. Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors instead.
notes.C: Alpha-adrenergic receptors respond to catecholamines and are not the target of atropine.
notes.D: Beta-2 receptor stimulation can dilate airways, but atropine's effect comes from blockade of a cholinergic receptor.
notes.E: H1 receptors mediate histamine-induced bronchoconstriction. Atropine does not act as an H1 antagonist.

phy-resp-597.why: Atropine can relax airways by preventing acetylcholine from activating smooth muscle muscarinic receptors. Its effect is greatest when existing bronchoconstrictor tone depends on vagal activity.

notes.A: Greater parasympathetic activity increases acetylcholine release and tends to narrow the bronchi.
notes.B: Acetylcholine stimulates muscarinic M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle and promotes contraction.
notes.C: Histamine can contract airway smooth muscle through H1 receptors, especially in susceptible airways.
notes.E: Atropine provides a mechanism for bronchodilation by removing muscarinic constrictor tone.

phy-resp-599.why: Irritants at the bronchial mucosa can activate sensory afferents and a vagal reflex. Acetylcholine released by parasympathetic efferents stimulates airway smooth muscle contraction.

notes.B: Beta-2 adrenoceptor stimulation raises cyclic AMP and favours relaxation of airway smooth muscle.
notes.C: Low alveolar oxygen classically constricts nearby pulmonary arterioles. That vascular response is distinct from the irritant reflex in bronchi.
notes.D: Warming inspired air to near body temperature is not a usual direct trigger for reflex bronchial constriction.
notes.E: Noradrenaline is less effective than epinephrine at bronchial beta-2 receptors and is not the usual trigger for irritant-induced bronchoconstriction.

phy-resp-614.why: Beta-2 receptor stimulation relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and can relieve the reversible bronchoconstriction of asthma. It acts on airflow limitation, which is distinct from controlling the underlying airway inflammation.

notes.A: Muscarinic cholinergic stimulation can increase airway smooth muscle contraction and aggravate airflow limitation.
notes.C: Inhaled histamine can provoke airway narrowing in people with airway hyperresponsiveness.
notes.D: NSAIDs do not provide direct bronchodilation and can provoke symptoms in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.
notes.E: Mineralocorticoids chiefly regulate electrolyte balance. The anti-inflammatory steroids used in asthma act through glucocorticoid pathways.

phy-resp-621.why: Histamine contracts bronchial smooth muscle chiefly by stimulating H1 receptors. This can narrow airways, particularly when bronchial responsiveness is increased.

notes.B: H2 receptors participate in other histamine actions, such as gastric acid secretion, but do not mediate the usual bronchial contraction.
notes.C: Muscarinic receptors are activated by acetylcholine, which also constricts airways through a separate pathway.
notes.D: Nicotinic receptors mediate neuronal or neuromuscular signalling and are not bronchial smooth muscle histamine receptors.
notes.E: Alpha-adrenergic receptors respond to catecholamines. Histamine does not act through them to contract bronchi.

phy-resp-623.why: Beta-2 adrenergic activation increases cyclic AMP in airway smooth muscle and promotes bronchodilation. Circulating epinephrine is an important physiological source of this signal in humans.

notes.B: Alpha-2 receptors are involved in other adrenergic effects, including regulation of transmitter release. They are not the main bronchial relaxant receptor.
notes.C: M1 is a muscarinic cholinergic receptor. The standard adrenergic bronchodilator effect is mediated by beta-2 receptors.
notes.D: Nicotinic receptors are important for transmission in autonomic ganglia. They do not mediate direct adrenergic relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle.
notes.E: Beta-2 receptors provide the relevant link between adrenergic stimulation and smooth muscle relaxation.

phy-resp-648.why: Histamine can increase bronchial smooth muscle tone through H1 receptors, especially in hyperresponsive airways. This narrows the airway lumen and can increase resistance.

notes.A: Adrenaline activates beta-2 receptors and usually favours bronchodilation.
notes.B: Noradrenaline is a weaker beta-2 agonist than adrenaline. It is not the classic mediator of histamine-like bronchial contraction.
notes.D: Atropine blocks muscarinic bronchoconstrictor tone and can therefore favour airway dilation.
notes.E: Curare blocks nicotinic neuromuscular transmission in skeletal muscle. It is not a normal mediator of bronchial smooth muscle contraction.

phy-resp-649.why: Catecholamines, particularly epinephrine, can enlarge bronchial calibre through beta-2 receptors on airway smooth muscle. This relaxant pathway acts through cyclic AMP.

notes.B: Acetylcholine increases bronchial smooth muscle tone primarily through muscarinic M3 receptors.
notes.C: Histamine can raise bronchial smooth muscle tone via H1 receptors and narrow airways.
notes.D: Bradykinin can trigger airway irritation and bronchoconstriction in susceptible individuals.
notes.E: Serotonin can contribute to airway constriction in some settings. It is not the usual catecholamine-mediated bronchodilator.

phy-resp-053.why: Most transported carbon dioxide is converted to bicarbonate. Red-cell carbonic anhydrase accelerates the reaction of carbon dioxide with water, and much of the resulting bicarbonate enters plasma in exchange for chloride.

notes.A: Dissolved carbon dioxide determines its partial pressure and is transported in blood, but it accounts for a minority of total carriage.
notes.B: Some carbon dioxide binds to globin to form carbaminohaemoglobin. This is a smaller fraction than bicarbonate transport.
notes.C: Carbonic acid is a short-lived intermediate that mainly dissociates to bicarbonate and hydrogen ions.
notes.E: Carbonic anhydrase catalyses carbon dioxide hydration. The enzyme is not a substantial form of carbon dioxide carriage.

phy-resp-054.why: Low alveolar oxygen constricts nearby pulmonary resistance vessels, diverting blood toward better ventilated alveoli. Systemic tissues usually respond to local hypoxia with vasodilation to increase oxygen delivery.

notes.A: Coronary vessels generally dilate when local oxygen delivery is inadequate relative to myocardial demand.
notes.C: Local hypoxia generally increases cerebral blood flow by dilating resistance vessels when severe enough.
notes.D: In active muscle, local metabolic signals including low oxygen favour vasodilation to increase delivery.
notes.E: Skin blood flow has strong thermal and autonomic regulation. It is not the classic example of local hypoxic vasoconstriction.

phy-resp-056.why: The pulmonary and systemic circulations carry essentially the same average flow because they are arranged in series. Pulmonary arterial pressure is lower because the pulmonary vascular bed has much lower resistance.

notes.A: The average flow pumped by the right and left sides of the heart is approximately the same over time.
notes.C: Pulmonary arterial pressure is normally substantially below systemic arterial pressure.
notes.D: The pulmonary capillary bed is normally a low-pressure system, which helps limit fluid movement into alveolar tissue.
notes.E: Cardiac output through the pulmonary circulation is approximately the same as systemic cardiac output at steady state.

phy-resp-057.why: When alveolar ventilation falls relative to metabolism, the lungs remove less carbon dioxide and alveolar PCO₂ rises. Alveolar oxygen then falls, which can cause both arterial hypercapnia and tissue hypoxia.

notes.A: Inadequate alveolar ventilation reduces carbon dioxide clearance and increases arterial PCO₂.
notes.B: Anoxia means nearly complete absence of oxygen. Hypoventilation can reduce oxygen substantially without eliminating it.
notes.C: As alveolar oxygen decreases, arterial oxygen can decrease and compromise tissue oxygen delivery.
notes.D: Hypocapnia is more typical of excessive alveolar ventilation relative to carbon dioxide production.

phy-resp-058.why: Increased tissue PCO₂ favours carbon dioxide hydration and hydrogen ion formation, lowering local pH. Both the higher carbon dioxide and lower pH reduce haemoglobin's oxygen affinity and promote unloading through the Bohr effect.

notes.A: Hydration of carbon dioxide generates hydrogen ions, so higher local PCO₂ usually lowers pH.
notes.B: Haemoglobin has lower oxygen affinity in acid, carbon dioxide-rich tissues, so more oxygen can unload at the same PO₂.
notes.C: Excess tissue carbon dioxide can be hydrated to bicarbonate and hydrogen ions, lowering local pH.
notes.D: High carbon dioxide often dilates systemic vessels, notably in the brain. The Bohr effect concerns oxygen binding rather than a general constrictor response.

phy-resp-062.why: The core respiratory functions of the lung are to move air into and out of alveoli and to allow oxygen and carbon dioxide to diffuse between alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood.

notes.A: Pulmonary vascular tone affects perfusion and matching to ventilation. It is distinct from moving air and transferring gases across the membrane.
notes.B: Ventilation is the renewal of alveolar gas that maintains the gradients for oxygen and carbon dioxide transfer.
notes.C: Diffusion is the process that transfers oxygen to blood and carbon dioxide into alveolar gas.
notes.D: The lung handles lipids in functions such as surfactant production. Lipid metabolism is distinct from respiratory gas exchange.

phy-resp-063.why: By Fick's law, gas transfer increases with surface area and decreases as the membrane gets thicker. The gas diffusion coefficient and the partial-pressure difference across the barrier also affect transfer.

notes.A: A thicker barrier increases the diffusion distance and decreases transfer at a fixed partial-pressure difference.
notes.B: A larger exchange area provides more parallel routes for diffusion and increases transfer.
notes.C: Tidal volume affects ventilation and can change alveolar partial pressures indirectly. It is not itself a dimension of the membrane.
notes.D: Residual volume is the gas left after maximal expiration, not a direct determinant of membrane diffusion in Fick's law.

phy-resp-064.why: Most gas exchange takes place across thin alveolar walls and the adjacent pulmonary capillaries. Oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses into the alveoli down their respective partial-pressure gradients.

notes.A: The trachea is a conducting airway and does not provide a substantial gas exchange surface.
notes.B: Bronchi conduct and distribute air. Their walls are not the main blood–gas barrier.
notes.C: Terminal bronchioles are conducting airways. Respiratory bronchioles have alveolar outpouchings that allow gas exchange.
notes.E: The larynx helps regulate airflow and phonation and does not provide an alveolar exchange surface.

phy-resp-065.why: In an upright lung, ventilation and perfusion both increase toward the base, but perfusion increases more steeply. Thus V/Q is higher at the apex. In prone positioning, the gravitational gradient is mainly ventral to dorsal and matching tends to be more uniform.

notes.A: The upright gradient in perfusion is steeper than the gradient in ventilation, so the ratio is higher at the apex.
notes.B: Regional ventilation generally increases toward the base of the upright lung, where resting alveoli have more room to expand.
notes.C: Perfusion is greater toward the dependent base in an upright person rather than increasing toward the apex.
notes.D: In a prone person, the main gravity-dependent axis is ventral to dorsal. An upright apex-to-base rule cannot simply be applied.

phy-resp-067.why: Conversion to bicarbonate accounts for most carbon dioxide transport, commonly estimated at about 70 percent of the total carried from tissues. Carbonic anhydrase in red cells accelerates hydration, and bicarbonate is exchanged for chloride across the red-cell membrane.

notes.A: Dissolved carbon dioxide accounts for a relatively small fraction of total carriage. It determines the measured partial pressure.
notes.B: Some carbon dioxide forms carbamino compounds, especially with haemoglobin, but this is less than the bicarbonate fraction.
notes.D: Bicarbonate is the predominant transport form, so an estimate of only ten percent is too low.
notes.E: Oxygenation decreases blood carbon dioxide carriage at a given PCO₂ through the Haldane effect.

phy-resp-071.why: The blood–gas barrier includes thin alveolar epithelial cells, capillary endothelial cells and their basement membranes, which are often fused. Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross this barrier by diffusion.

notes.A: The epithelial and endothelial layers and their associated basement membranes constitute the thin structural barrier.
notes.B: Oxygen and carbon dioxide move in opposite directions along their own partial-pressure gradients.
notes.C: Carbon dioxide is much more soluble in tissue fluid and has greater membrane diffusivity than oxygen at an equal pressure gradient.
notes.E: The stated structural layers and the capacity for oxygen and carbon dioxide diffusion are both features of the barrier.

phy-resp-080.why: Increased carbon dioxide and the resulting fall in pH lower haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen. The curve shifts right, meaning more oxygen is released at a given tissue PO₂.

notes.B: Lower carbon dioxide tends to increase haemoglobin oxygen affinity and shift the curve left.
notes.C: A fall in PO₂ changes saturation by moving along a given curve. It does not by itself shift the curve.
notes.D: Increasing PO₂ increases saturation along the existing curve when other conditions are fixed.
notes.E: Higher pH increases oxygen affinity and tends to produce a left shift.

phy-resp-580.why: Carboxyhaemoglobin forms when carbon monoxide binds to haem iron. Carbon dioxide is carried primarily as bicarbonate, partly dissolved, and partly as carbamino groups attached to proteins such as haemoglobin.

notes.A: Carbaminohaemoglobin is formed when carbon dioxide binds to amino groups on globin.
notes.C: Bicarbonate is the principal form of carbon dioxide carriage in blood, mostly dissolved in plasma.
notes.D: Some carbon dioxide is carried in physical solution. This fraction determines the partial pressure that drives exchange.
notes.E: Both carbamino compounds and physically dissolved carbon dioxide make real contributions to transport.

phy-resp-585.why: Oxygen crosses cell membranes by simple diffusion, moving from higher to lower oxygen partial pressure. Cellular consumption maintains the gradient from the extracellular fluid toward the mitochondria.

notes.B: Filtration is driven by a pressure difference that moves fluid and some solutes through a barrier. It is not the usual route for cellular oxygen entry.
notes.C: Osmosis refers to net water movement driven by solute differences. Oxygen itself diffuses down its partial-pressure gradient.
notes.D: Oxygen entry does not require ATP-dependent pumps. It follows a gradient maintained by oxygen utilisation.
notes.E: Oxygen can pass through the lipid bilayer without requiring a specific membrane carrier.

phy-resp-586.why: Most tissue carbon dioxide is converted to bicarbonate inside red cells. Bicarbonate then moves into plasma in exchange for chloride, so most carbon dioxide reaches the lungs in this ionic form.

notes.A: Carbon dioxide can be dissolved molecularly in plasma, but it is not carried as bubbles during normal circulation.
notes.B: Carbon dioxide bound to haemoglobin forms carbaminohaemoglobin, a minority of the total carried.
notes.D: Plasma proteins can carry a small amount of carbon dioxide, but this is not the main transport mechanism.
notes.E: Circulating blood is the principal transport system for carbon dioxide going to the lungs.

phy-resp-588.why: Pulmonary gas exchange occurs across the interface between alveolar air and blood in pulmonary capillaries. The capillary network lies close to the alveolar wall and provides a large surface for diffusion.

notes.A: Terminal bronchioles are conducting airways. Respiratory bronchioles can exchange gas through alveoli opening from their walls.
notes.B: The bronchi conduct air to smaller airways but do not normally provide the thin alveolar–capillary exchange surface.
notes.D: The lung roots transmit bronchi, vessels and nerves. The gas exchange interface is distributed throughout the alveolar tissue.
notes.E: The trachea carries air toward the lungs, where exchange occurs at the alveolar surface.

phy-resp-590.why: Lower pH reduces haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen through the Bohr effect. At a given tissue PO₂, acidic conditions therefore favour oxygen unloading.

notes.B: Higher pH increases haemoglobin oxygen affinity and makes it less likely to release oxygen at the same PO₂.
notes.C: Cooling generally increases oxygen affinity. It tends to oppose, rather than promote, unloading.
notes.D: Openness is not a physiological determinant of haemoglobin affinity. Local pH and PCO₂ are directly relevant.
notes.E: Acidity provides a specific mechanism by which metabolising tissue can increase oxygen delivery.

phy-resp-598.why: Both ventilation and perfusion decrease toward the apex of an upright lung. Because perfusion falls relatively more, ventilation per unit of perfusion is higher at the apex than at the base.

notes.A: Typical resting alveolar ventilation is about four litres per minute and pulmonary blood flow is about five, giving a ratio below one.
notes.B: Alveolar ventilation and perfusion both rise during exercise. A ratio below 0.6 is not the usual general result of maximal exercise.
notes.D: Oxygen moves passively across the alveolar–capillary barrier down its partial-pressure gradient.
notes.E: Conducting airways can expand during inspiration. A decrease in anatomical dead space is not a general feature of inspiration.

phy-resp-601.why: Most carbon dioxide is transported as bicarbonate. In tissue capillaries, red-cell carbonic anhydrase accelerates bicarbonate formation. The reaction runs in reverse in the lungs so carbon dioxide can be exhaled.

notes.B: Carbaminohaemoglobin carries a minority of carbon dioxide by binding it to globin amino groups.
notes.C: The physically dissolved gas accounts for a small fraction and establishes the partial pressure.
notes.D: Plasma proteins can form carbamino compounds, but the bulk of carbon dioxide is carried as bicarbonate.
notes.E: Carbon dioxide can bind to globin amino groups. Haem iron is the site for oxygen binding.

phy-resp-606.why: Resting mean pulmonary arterial pressure is commonly about 15 mm Hg versus a systemic mean near 90 mm Hg. The pulmonary circulation carries roughly the same flow at lower pressure because it has far lower vascular resistance.

notes.B: Both circuits are in series and have nearly equal minute blood flow at steady state.
notes.C: Pulmonary vascular resistance is typically much less than half systemic resistance. The pressure drop is low despite similar flow.
notes.D: The systemic vascular bed, especially its veins, contains a much larger fraction of total blood volume.
notes.E: During increased flow, pulmonary vessels can recruit and distend, limiting the rise in pressure compared with the increase in cardiac output.

phy-resp-607.why: The largest share of blood carbon dioxide is carried as bicarbonate. Red cells catalyse bicarbonate formation, and much of it then moves into plasma through the chloride exchange mechanism.

notes.A: Myoglobin is chiefly an intracellular oxygen-binding protein in muscle and is not a major circulating carbon dioxide carrier.
notes.B: Plasma proteins can carry some carbamino carbon dioxide, but this is a small fraction of total carriage.
notes.C: Some gas is physically dissolved in red cells and plasma. Dissolved carbon dioxide is a minority of the total.
notes.D: Much bicarbonate formed inside red cells is exchanged into plasma, which carries most of the bicarbonate fraction.

phy-resp-608.why: A right shift reduces haemoglobin oxygen affinity and raises the PO₂ needed for half saturation. At a given tissue PO₂, haemoglobin therefore releases more oxygen.

notes.A: In pulmonary capillaries, removal of carbon dioxide helps increase affinity and supports oxygen loading. A right shift is more characteristic of metabolically active tissues.
notes.B: Cooling increases haemoglobin affinity and usually shifts the curve left instead of right.
notes.D: A right shift lowers saturation at the same PO₂ and favours unloading. It does not itself enhance binding in the lungs.
notes.E: Higher pH increases oxygen affinity and produces a left shift through the Bohr relationship.

phy-resp-611.why: Carbon dioxide diffuses across the blood–gas barrier about 20 times more readily than oxygen for the same partial-pressure gradient. Its much greater solubility more than offsets its greater molecular mass.

notes.A: The gases have different membrane diffusivities, primarily because carbon dioxide is much more soluble.
notes.B: The comparison is reversed. Carbon dioxide has the higher diffusion coefficient across the respiratory membrane.
notes.D: Raising the oxygen gradient increases its actual flux, but that does not change oxygen's diffusion coefficient relative to carbon dioxide.
notes.E: Membrane permeability is one determinant of gas transfer, along with area, thickness and the partial-pressure gradient.

phy-resp-613.why: At a given PCO₂, oxygenated blood carries less total carbon dioxide than deoxygenated blood. Oxygenation reduces carbamino binding and reduces haemoglobin's capacity to buffer hydrogen ions, which favours carbon dioxide release in the lungs.

notes.A: The whole-blood carbon dioxide content curve is relatively close to linear over the physiological range. The familiar sigmoid curve describes oxygen saturation.
notes.B: Carbon dioxide content continues to increase as PCO₂ rises in the usual physiological range. There is no nearby saturation plateau.
notes.C: At equilibrium, a PCO₂ approaching zero greatly reduces the dissolved carbon dioxide and the carbon dioxide-dependent forms of carriage.
notes.E: Added carbon dioxide can reduce oxygen affinity through the Bohr effect. The carbon dioxide dissociation curve directly illustrates the effect of oxygenation on carbon dioxide content.

phy-resp-618.why: A left shift increases haemoglobin oxygen affinity. At the same tissue PO₂, more oxygen remains bound to haemoglobin and less is unloaded.

notes.A: Increased affinity means the oxygen content is generally higher at the same PO₂, assuming the same haemoglobin concentration.
notes.C: Higher temperature decreases haemoglobin oxygen affinity and generally shifts the curve to the right.
notes.D: A lower pH favours oxygen release and shifts the curve right through the Bohr effect.
notes.E: Fetal haemoglobin has higher oxygen affinity than adult haemoglobin, so its curve is the one shifted left.

phy-resp-624.why: Lowering V/Q throughout both lungs reduces alveolar oxygen relative to perfusion and generally lowers arterial oxygen content. It can also impair carbon dioxide clearance if total alveolar ventilation is reduced.

notes.B: Lower alveolar PO₂ reduces end-capillary oxygen saturation, making unchanged systemic oxygen content unlikely without other compensation.
notes.C: Low V/Q means perfusion exceeds relative ventilation. Dead space is associated with ventilation of poorly perfused regions instead.
notes.D: Widespread hypoventilation increases arterial PCO₂ if carbon dioxide production remains constant.
notes.E: Both lungs are affected in the stem, so there is no unaffected contralateral lung with a high ratio to compensate.

phy-resp-625.why: Oxygen delivery is arterial oxygen content multiplied by cardiac output. Normally well over 95 percent of the arterial oxygen content is bound to haemoglobin, while only a small amount is dissolved.

notes.A: Tissue oxygen consumption is only the portion extracted from delivered blood. Unused oxygen returns in venous blood.
notes.C: Halving haemoglobin lowers oxygen content if saturation is unchanged, but delivery may be partly maintained by increased cardiac output.
notes.D: Oxygen content depends strongly on haemoglobin concentration and saturation. PO₂ chiefly determines the small dissolved fraction and helps set saturation.
notes.E: Increased consumption can be met by increasing oxygen extraction as well as delivery, so delivery need not increase in exact proportion.
